sections.guidingQuestion: Which neuronal structure commonly conducts action potentials over long distances?
sections.explanation:
A neuron has a cell body containing cytoplasm and a nucleus. Multiple shorter dendrites commonly receive inputs, while a single elongated axon carries impulses toward its terminal branches. Fibre lengths and cell shape vary with function.

Nerve fibres conduct electrical impulses through changes in membrane voltage caused by ion movement. At a terminal, an impulse can trigger communication to another neuron or an effector such as muscle. A nerve is a bundle of fibres from many neurons, not one large cell.

sections.guidingQuestion: What directly sustains Na⁺ and K⁺ concentration gradients over time?
sections.explanation:
The sodium–potassium pump uses ATP to transport three Na⁺ out and two K⁺ into a neuron per cycle. This maintains a higher Na⁺ concentration outside and a higher K⁺ concentration inside. The unequal pumping also makes a small direct contribution to membrane voltage.

At rest, the membrane is more permeable to K⁺ than to Na⁺. K⁺ can diffuse out through leak channels, leaving the inside relatively negative; electrical attraction then opposes further K⁺ loss. A voltage difference across the membrane is polarization. Around −70 mV is a common illustrative resting potential, not a value shared by every neuron. Pumps maintain the gradients, while selective permeability is central to the resting voltage.
sections.revisionSummary: The Na⁺/K⁺ pump uses ATP to move three Na⁺ out and two K⁺ in, maintaining ion concentration gradients. Greater resting K⁺ permeability allows outward K⁺ diffusion, leaving the inside relatively negative.
terms: Resting potential: voltage difference across an unstimulated neuron's membrane
sections.workedExample: If ATP production stops for long enough, ion gradients erode and normal excitability is lost.

sections.guidingQuestion: What carries the local current involved in nerve impulses?
sections.explanation:
A nerve impulse is an action potential: a brief change in membrane voltage caused by movement of charged ions across the membrane. The signal is electrical because ions carry charge; it is not a stream of electrons travelling down a wire.

An action potential triggers a new voltage change in the adjacent excitable membrane, so it propagates along the fibre without progressively losing amplitude under normal conditions. The same sodium ions do not travel the entire length of the axon. Detailed channel timing and local-current mechanisms are additional HL.
sections.revisionSummary: Movement of charged ions across the membrane changes membrane voltage. The action potential is regenerated in successive excitable regions rather than progressively fading.
terms: Action potential: brief self-propagating reversal in membrane potential

A larger axon has lower internal resistance to current spread and generally conducts faster. Squid giant axons illustrate increased speed in large unmyelinated fibres compared with smaller unmyelinated fibres. Myelination increases speed further compared with similarly sized unmyelinated fibres.

Positive r means the measured variables tend to increase together; negative r means one tends to decrease as the other increases. Larger |r| indicates a stronger linear association. In an illustrative simple linear regression with an intercept, r = +0.80 gives R² = 0.64: the fitted model accounts for 64% of the observed variation in speed. A negative r = −0.60 gives R² = 0.36. sections.guidingQuestion: What makes a typical chemical synapse directional?
sections.explanation:
A synapse joins a neuron to another neuron or an effector such as muscle or a gland. The presynaptic terminal contains neurotransmitter vesicles; a synaptic cleft separates it from the postsynaptic membrane, which has receptors.

The presynaptic cell releases neurotransmitter, which diffuses across the cleft and binds postsynaptic receptors. This arrangement normally allows signalling in one direction. An electrical impulse travels along the axon, while a chemical messenger crosses the synaptic cleft.

sections.guidingQuestion: What ion enters the terminal and triggers neurotransmitter exocytosis?
sections.explanation:
An arriving action potential depolarizes the presynaptic membrane, opening voltage-gated calcium channels. Ca²⁺ enters down its electrochemical gradient and acts as a signalling chemical inside the terminal.

The rise in cytoplasmic calcium promotes fusion of neurotransmitter-filled vesicles with the presynaptic membrane. Neurotransmitter is released by exocytosis and diffuses across the cleft. Calcium is the intracellular release signal, not the neurotransmitter carried to the next cell.

sections.guidingQuestion: What is an excitatory postsynaptic potential?
sections.explanation:
Acetylcholine diffuses across the synaptic cleft and binds transmembrane receptors on the postsynaptic cell. At an excitatory cholinergic synapse, receptor-linked cation channels open, producing a net inward positive current near resting voltage.

The postsynaptic membrane becomes less negative, producing a graded excitatory postsynaptic potential (EPSP). An EPSP need not reach threshold by itself; sufficient depolarization can trigger an action potential. Acetylcholine acts at many synapses, including neuromuscular junctions, where the receiving cell is muscle. Removal or breakdown of transmitter limits the signal.

sections.guidingQuestion: Which ion current principally drives the rapid upstroke?
sections.explanation:
When threshold is reached, voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open rapidly. Na⁺ enters, causing further depolarization and opening more channels by positive feedback. The membrane potential rises and can briefly become positive.

Na⁺ channels inactivate while slower voltage-gated K⁺ channels open; K⁺ leaves and repolarizes the membrane. Delayed K⁺ channel closure can cause an after-hyperpolarization. Sodium-channel inactivation and recovery underlie the absolute refractory period. The pump maintains ion gradients over many impulses; it does not cause the rapid falling phase, and a single impulse does not reverse the bulk Na⁺ and K⁺ concentrations.

sections.guidingQuestion: What allows an action potential to move along the axon?
sections.explanation:
Na⁺ entry makes an active axon region more positive inside. Local charge movement spreads to adjacent resting regions inside the axon, with return current outside, depolarizing nearby membrane toward threshold.

At threshold, voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open in the next region, generating a new action potential. Recently activated channels behind the wave are temporarily inactivated, limiting immediate backward re-excitation. Propagation recruits successive membrane regions; it does not carry one parcel of sodium from cell body to terminal.
sections.revisionSummary: Na⁺ entry creates local current inside the axon, with return current outside, depolarizing adjacent membrane. Reaching threshold opens voltage-gated Na⁺ channels there and regenerates the action potential.
terms: Local current: charge movement from an excited axon region toward neighbouring membrane
sections.workedExample: A stimulated mid-axon region can initially send action potentials in both directions, but normal initiation at the axon initial segment propagates toward terminals.

sections.guidingQuestion: Where are action potentials regenerated along a myelinated axon?
sections.explanation:
Schwann cells in the peripheral nervous system and oligodendrocytes in the central nervous system wrap parts of axons in myelin. The insulated segments are called internodes; gaps between them are the nodes of Ranvier. Myelin greatly reduces leakage of electrical current through covered membrane, whereas voltage-gated ion channels and ion pumps are concentrated at the exposed nodes.

An action potential at one node allows inward Na⁺ current. The resulting local depolarizing current spreads through the axoplasm along the myelinated internode and raises the voltage of the next node toward threshold. At threshold, clustered voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open and regenerate an action potential at that node. The current crosses the internode electrically; the action potential is actively renewed at successive nodes, not teleported through air.

In an unmyelinated axon, nearby sections of membrane must repeatedly depolarize as the impulse advances. In a myelinated axon, active regeneration is concentrated at the nodes while local current spreads rapidly through insulated regions. This typically increases conduction speed and reduces the amount of membrane undergoing large ion movements. Pumps maintain ion gradients over time, but they do not create the rapid rising phase of each action potential.

sections.guidingQuestion: Why is consciousness classified as emergent?
sections.explanation:
Individual neurons generate impulses and communicate at synapses. Networks integrate sensory information, memory and other activity through many coordinated interactions. Their collective functions are not properties of one isolated neuron.

It does not imply that every mechanism of subjective awareness is fully understood or that one settled theory must be learned.

options.text: The axon lacks a plasma membrane
options.feedback: An axon requires a plasma membrane with ion channels to conduct an action potential.

options.text: Both cells must release transmitter simultaneously
options.feedback: A typical chemical synapse does not need both cells to release transmitter at the same time.

options.text: The cleft is filled with DNA
options.feedback: The cleft contains extracellular fluid across which transmitter diffuses, not a DNA bridge.

questions.prompt: Explain why a typical chemical synapse transmits in one direction. [2]
questions.answer: Neurotransmitter vesicles and release machinery are presynaptic. Receptors are postsynaptic, so released transmitter diffuses from the releasing side to the receiving side.
markingPoints: Neurotransmitter vesicles and release machinery are presynaptic.
Receptors are postsynaptic, so released transmitter diffuses from the releasing side to the receiving side.

questions.prompt: What ion enters the terminal and triggers neurotransmitter exocytosis?

options.feedback: Ca²⁺ enters via voltage-gated channels and triggers vesicle fusion at the presynaptic terminal.
Chloride movement can modify membrane potential, but Ca²⁺ is the principal exocytosis trigger.
Molecular oxygen is not a calcium-like charged signalling ion that directly triggers vesicle fusion.
DNA is a macromolecule and does not pass through presynaptic calcium channels.

questions.prompt: Explain how presynaptic depolarization causes neurotransmitter release. [2]
questions.answer: Depolarization opens voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels and calcium enters the terminal. Calcium acts as an intracellular signal promoting vesicle fusion and neurotransmitter exocytosis.
markingPoints: Depolarization opens voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels and calcium enters the terminal.
Calcium acts as an intracellular signal promoting vesicle fusion and neurotransmitter exocytosis.

questions.prompt: What is an excitatory postsynaptic potential?

options.text: A graded depolarization that increases action-potential likelihood
options.feedback: An EPSP is a small graded depolarization that makes reaching threshold more likely.

options.text: An obligatory negative shift far below rest
options.feedback: A negative shift below rest is characteristic of hyperpolarization, not an excitatory depolarization.

options.text: A DNA copy generated after every synapse
options.feedback: Synaptic transmission changes membrane conductance rapidly; it does not require copying DNA each time.

options.text: Movement of insulin into the nucleus
options.feedback: Insulin nuclear transport is unrelated to the graded electrical response at an excitatory synapse.

questions.prompt: Explain how acetylcholine can generate an EPSP. [2]
questions.answer: It diffuses across the cleft and binds postsynaptic transmembrane receptors. Receptor-linked cation channels allow net positive charge entry, depolarizing the membrane toward threshold.
markingPoints: It diffuses across the cleft and binds postsynaptic transmembrane receptors.
Receptor-linked cation channels allow net positive charge entry, depolarizing the membrane toward threshold.

questions.prompt: Which ion current principally drives the rapid upstroke?

options.feedback: Opening voltage-gated Na⁺ channels generates the rapid depolarizing current.
ATP synthase is not a potassium-entry channel; K⁺ efflux through voltage-gated channels helps repolarize.
Steroid receptors regulate signalling or transcription, not the action-potential sodium upstroke.
GLUT4 transports glucose and is not an electrogenic channel for the fast upstroke.

questions.prompt: Explain the rising and falling phases of an action potential. [2]
questions.answer: Threshold opens voltage-gated Na⁺ channels, allowing Na⁺ influx and rapid depolarization. Na⁺ channels inactivate and voltage-gated K⁺ channels open; K⁺ efflux repolarizes the membrane.
markingPoints: Threshold opens voltage-gated Na⁺ channels, allowing Na⁺ influx and rapid depolarization.
Na⁺ channels inactivate and voltage-gated K⁺ channels open; K⁺ efflux repolarizes the membrane.

questions.prompt: What allows an action potential to move along the axon?

options.text: Local currents depolarize adjacent membrane to threshold
options.feedback: Local ionic current depolarizes adjacent axon membrane until voltage-gated channels regenerate the impulse.

options.text: One packet of Na⁺ moves untouched from one end to the other
options.feedback: An impulse is renewed in successive membrane regions; the identical ions do not travel the entire axon.

options.text: Glucose channels open in every region
options.feedback: Glucose transport is not the event that regenerates neighbouring membrane action potentials.

options.text: Neurotransmitter diffuses inside the whole axon
options.feedback: Neurotransmitters diffuse across synapses, not as the propagating electrical carrier inside an entire axon.

questions.prompt: Explain propagation of an action potential by local currents. [2]
questions.answer: Na⁺ entry creates local current inside the axon, with return current outside, depolarizing adjacent membrane. Reaching threshold opens voltage-gated Na⁺ channels there and regenerates the action potential.
markingPoints: Na⁺ entry creates local current inside the axon, with return current outside, depolarizing adjacent membrane.
Reaching threshold opens voltage-gated Na⁺ channels there and regenerates the action potential.

questions.prompt: What is the frequency of five action potentials in 0.25 s?

options.feedback: Frequency is count divided by time: 5 ÷ 0.25 s = 20 impulses s⁻¹ = 20 Hz.
1.25 is the product 5 × 0.25, not impulses divided by elapsed time.
Millivolts measure voltage, whereas frequency requires reciprocal seconds (Hz).
0.05 Hz is not 5/0.25; divide impulse count by the time interval in seconds.

questions.prompt: Five action potentials are recorded in 250 ms. Calculate the firing frequency and show the time conversion. [2]
markingPoints: Frequency = 5 ÷ 0.250 = 20 Hz.

questions.prompt: Where are action potentials regenerated along a myelinated axon?

options.feedback: Voltage-gated Na⁺ channels clustered at nodes regenerate action potentials between myelinated segments.
Compact myelin insulates internodes, where the same density of regenerative channels is absent.
The nucleus processes gene expression; it is not an axonal site where impulses regenerate.
Mitochondria help supply ATP, but the action-potential spike is regenerated at nodal membrane.

questions.prompt: Explain how myelin and nodes of Ranvier increase conduction speed. [2]
questions.answer: Myelin limits current leakage so local depolarizing current spreads rapidly along internodes. Channels concentrated at nodes regenerate action potentials node to node, rather than at every small membrane region.
markingPoints: Myelin limits current leakage so local depolarizing current spreads rapidly along internodes.
Channels concentrated at nodes regenerate action potentials node to node, rather than at every small membrane region.

questions.prompt: How does cocaine chiefly modify monoamine synaptic signalling?

options.feedback: Cocaine inhibits monoamine reuptake transporters, leaving more transmitter in the synaptic space.
Cocaine does not transform dopamine into ATP; the effect concerns membrane uptake of transmitter.

options.text: It blocks every postsynaptic ion channel irreversibly
options.feedback: It does not irreversibly shut every postsynaptic ion channel; its central effect is transporter inhibition.
Changes in myelin thickness are not the acute mechanism of cocaine's synaptic effects.

questions.prompt: Compare the sites of action of neonicotinoids and cocaine in synaptic transmission. [2]
questions.answer: Neonicotinoids act on insect nicotinic acetylcholine receptors, disrupting normal transmission. Cocaine inhibits transmitter reuptake transporters, prolonging transmitter presence and signalling.
markingPoints: Neonicotinoids act on insect nicotinic acetylcholine receptors, disrupting normal transmission.
Cocaine inhibits transmitter reuptake transporters, prolonging transmitter presence and signalling.

questions.prompt: What is the typical effect of an IPSP?

options.text: Reduced likelihood of reaching action-potential threshold
options.feedback: An IPSP usually hyperpolarizes or shunts membrane responses, decreasing firing likelihood.

options.text: Guaranteed extra firing regardless of excitation
options.feedback: Inhibitory signalling reduces, rather than guarantees, reaching threshold after excitation.
Insulin secretion is endocrine physiology, not the direct definition of a postsynaptic inhibitory potential.

options.text: Production of a larger neuron nucleus
options.feedback: Cell-nucleus size does not explain a transient change in postsynaptic membrane potential.

questions.prompt: Explain how an inhibitory neurotransmitter reduces the chance of an action potential in the IB model. [2]
questions.answer: Its postsynaptic effect is hyperpolarization, making the membrane more negative. This moves membrane voltage farther from threshold and counteracts excitation.
markingPoints: Its postsynaptic effect is hyperpolarization, making the membrane more negative.
This moves membrane voltage farther from threshold and counteracts excitation.

questions.prompt: What describes spatial summation?

options.text: Combining signals from different synapses at similar times
options.feedback: Spatial summation combines postsynaptic potentials from several synapses at approximately the same time.

options.text: Repeated signals from one synapse over time
options.feedback: Repeated inputs from one synapse across time illustrate temporal, not spatial, summation.
Sodium pumping into a nucleus is unrelated to integration of inputs at the neuronal membrane.

options.text: A signal crossing a myelin membrane
options.feedback: A signal passing along a myelinated axon is conduction, not summation at synaptic inputs.

questions.prompt: Explain how excitatory and inhibitory inputs determine whether a postsynaptic neuron fires. [2]
questions.answer: Their graded effects combine according to strength and timing at the trigger region. If the net depolarization reaches threshold an all-or-nothing action potential is produced; inhibition may prevent this.
markingPoints: Their graded effects combine according to strength and timing at the trigger region.
If the net depolarization reaches threshold an all-or-nothing action potential is produced; inhibition may prevent this.

questions.prompt: What directly starts excitation of a capsaicin-sensitive free nerve ending?

options.feedback: Capsaicin can activate sensory cation channels, depolarizing a free nerve ending.
Liver hormone release is not the direct first event when a cutaneous nerve ending detects capsaicin.

options.text: Myelin synthesis at the skin surface
options.feedback: Myelin production does not transduce a noxious chemical stimulus at the nerve ending.

options.text: Insulin binding to a synaptic vesicle
options.feedback: Insulin-receptor binding is unrelated to the capsaicin-sensitive sensory ion channel.

questions.prompt: Explain how capsaicin at a skin nerve ending can lead to pain perception. [2]
questions.answer: Capsaicin opens stimulus-sensitive cation channels; positive-ion entry depolarizes the ending to threshold and initiates impulses. Signals pass to the brain through sensory pathways, where pain is perceived.
markingPoints: Capsaicin opens stimulus-sensitive cation channels; positive-ion entry depolarizes the ending to threshold and initiates impulses.
Signals pass to the brain through sensory pathways, where pain is perceived.

questions.prompt: Why is consciousness classified as emergent?

options.text: Network interactions produce system properties absent from an isolated neuron
options.feedback: Coordinated activity of neuronal networks produces system-level properties not present in one neuron alone.

options.text: Each neuron independently generates full awareness
options.feedback: An individual neuron does not independently contain the full integrated experience of consciousness.
Consciousness is associated with brain-network activity, not the complete absence of neuronal signalling.

options.text: Every action potential has identical personal meaning
options.feedback: Meaningful perception depends on patterns and network context; identical spikes do not each encode an identical experience.

questions.prompt: Explain why consciousness is described as an emergent property. [2]
questions.answer: It depends on coordinated interactions among many neurons in brain networks. The integrated capacities of the network are not present in one isolated neuron.
markingPoints: It depends on coordinated interactions among many neurons in brain networks.
The integrated capacities of the network are not present in one isolated neuron.

questions.prompt: An oscilloscope trace has six action-potential peaks during a 0.30 s observation window. Their individual heights are approximately +30 mV. Calculate impulse frequency, specify the unit, and explain why a stronger sustained stimulus typically alters frequency rather than spike amplitude. [5]

data.caption: Invented trace summary; approximate positive peak is not an exact universal spike voltage.

questions.answer: Frequency = 6/0.30 s = 20 Hz. Once threshold is reached, a spike is regenerative and approximately all-or-nothing; stimulus intensity can alter spike frequency. The +30 mV value is voltage, not frequency.
markingPoints: Use impulses divided by time.
Calculate 6/0.30 = 20.
Give Hz or s⁻¹ as the unit of frequency.
Voltage-gated channel opening produces regenerative, approximately all-or-nothing action potentials.
A stronger stimulus often recruits more spikes per unit time, not a proportionally higher membrane-voltage peak.
